utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. Welcome back. Mr. Hannis, we had not expected this pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's nice to be here. I hope you can still call it a pleasure at the end of my term here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our first witness today will be Milan Djakovic. We had initially proposed him as a 92 ter witness. Your Honours decided that he should be called viva voce. I think our time estimate for him previously was three hours. In light of the change from ter to viva, I think it may take me a little longer, but I propose to end my examination by the end of the day. I hope that meets with your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We look forward to the witness who may be brought in now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, I understand you're retired from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you retired and at what rank.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 31st of March, 2002, with the rank of lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long were you a professional soldier, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a professional soldier from the 31st July 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what position you held in the VJ and where you were working in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I was at the Pristina garrison of the Pristina Corps, discharging the duty of the head of operations and training department of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was your commanding officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was General Vladimir Lazarevic, holding the position of the head of -- Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Pristina Corps in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps commander was General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what your duties were as head of operations and training department in Pristina Corps at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My duties in 1998 when I assumed the duty of the head of department on the 25th of December, year 1997, and I held this position until February 2009 [sic] -- that is when I handed over my duties, and I was transferred to the 3rd Army command in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. The transcript reported you as saying you held that position until February 2009. I think that was probably a misinterpretation, because I understand you retired in 2002 so ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was retired in 2002. I don't understand what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The transcript reports that you said you held your position as head of the operations and training section or department until February 2009. I think that probably should be --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: 1999. I may have misspoken. So until February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Until I went to Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you went to Nis in February 1999, what was your job there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My job was similar to the one I had with the Pristina Corps, only for the most part of the time I remained in Pristina throughout 1999 at the forward command post in the village of Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. General, the first topic I want to talk with you about is something called the Joint Command in Kosovo and Metohija. And can you tell us the first time that you saw or heard that term used, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: For the first time we used this term, or it was mentioned in a conversation between General Pavkovic and myself. That took place sometime in the period -- or rather, in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you an exhibit, it is I think 65 ter number 02113. It will be coming up on your screen in a minute, sir. And this is a document dated the 7th of July, 1998, from the brigade commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see there in the first paragraph, this is entitled: "A ban on operations without knowledge and approval of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." And this order from the commander of the 125th is made apparently pursuant to the order of the Joint Command number 1104-6. Can you tell us about that? Do you know anything about that reference to a Joint Command and a Joint Command order of 6 July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This order dated the 6th of July, as far as I can recall, was drafted by myself; and in this order much before any events that involved civilians, members of the Ministry of the Interior and the engagement of the army, we in a certain manner and in order to re-affirm the joint coordination between MUP staff and the army, we mentioned this Joint Command as a notion or as a term that was suitable at the time from the point of view of drafting documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This -- what we have on the screen is an order from the commander of the 125th apparently to his subordinate units; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he's citing his authority, the order he received is 1104-6. Does that number mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't mean anything particular as a number. It's a number from the register -- from the register. And I asked for a number from the head of the administrative office, the next number that is in the register, in order to make references in the correspondence between us and the MUP with a view to coordinating certain activities. And this number 1104 is quite accidental, and this number 6 that comes after that is just the sequence number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how much you may have heard from other witnesses about the numbering system of VJ documents, so if I'm starting to go into something that you're well aware of, stop me and I'll break off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have not gone too far yet, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, as I understand it from having looked at a lot of VJ documents and heard from some other witnesses, that documents that were used in the VJ would have a registry number assigned based on sort of the topic of what the communication was about. And then, as you said, there would be that number, it was a random number; and after that, if there were multiple communications concerning that topic, they would get a sequential number. Oftentimes it might be followed then by a slash with the year. For example, if the topic was equipment in Kosovo, the number might be 123, the first communication about that would be dash 01, and then slash forward 98. Have I described it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if 1104 related to the Joint Command in some way, would -- does that mean there would have been five other communications about the Joint Command before this 1104-6?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said -- I think you referred to "we" as having been the ones who produced this document. Who are you referring to when you say "we" in that context?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1104 specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to the operations organ of the Pristina Corps command and some input of General Pavkovic was also taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And could we see the second page of this document. Did you know who the commander of the 125th was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was Colonel Dragan Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the second page do you recognise the name and the signature that's on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I never paid much attention to the signature, but I'm aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender 02113 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And next I'd like to -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document would become Exhibit P1216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I would like to show you Exhibit P886, which has previously been marked for identification I believe. General, you have the cover page of a lengthy document in front of you. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the title page is translated in English as: "Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the first page that I wrote on the 22nd of July, 2008 [sic] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is what the witness said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when we attended the meeting with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. The interpreters just told me that you said July 22nd of 2008. I think that was a misspeak --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you continue from where I interrupted you, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to attend this meeting pursuant to what General Pavkovic, when he returned from Belgrade on the 20th of July, he summoned me to come on the 22nd of July in the morning and told me that I was going to accompany him at the meeting with the MUP. When I asked him what I was supposed to do, he told me to, Come with me, so that he wouldn't be alone there, by that he was referring to VJ officers. When I asked whether I should bring something with me, he replied, Just bring a notebook with you and note down whatever you believe to be of interest for us. This is what I did. And on the 22nd of July, in the evening, at around 1800 or 1830, the aide-de-camp called me and asked me if I was ready. I said that I was. And then 15 minutes before this recorded time we arrived on the MUP premises which was about 100 metres from our command headquarters. The meeting started exactly at this time recorded here, which is 1900 hours. It started rather informally. Since I was not familiar and acquainted at all of the attendees, I skipped the entire half of the page without noting anything, without saying the meeting of the Joint Command and the agenda and the persons present. I added that afterwards, based on the fact that General Pavkovic and I, myself, established together upon our return to the command HQ. I started taking notes from this sentence which says that Mr. Minic opened the meeting, and I went on recording as much as I could what everyone was talking about, the propositions and proposals that were made, the information that was exchanged during the next 60-odd meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those -- how often did the group meet approximately during the time that you attended meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the average we met two to three times a week, depending on the intensity of the influx of information, the intensity of combat activities, et cetera. But I would say two or three times a week on the average.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were the meetings usually held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings, or rather, the first one was held in the building of the MUP, and for the most part they were held in a building in the centre of Pristina. I think that was in the provisional Executive Council, and the room was in size similar to this one, although some of the meetings between the MUP and the army were held when we had to deal some issues that were exclusively relating to our coordination; and then in that case we would hold them either on the premises of the corps or on the premises of the Ministry of the Interior. However, the majority of the meetings were held in the building of the provincial Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see on the page we have in front of us that at this first meeting you list eight people in attendance, including yourself and General Pavkovic. The other six, were these people known to you before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, no. I knew of Mr. Minic from the media, and I knew that he held a high political position. As for Mr. Sainovic, the same applies to him. I didn't know Mr. Djordjevic personally. I knew Lukic because already in June and July, or rather, late June he was already down there at the MUP staff, and I knew him. I didn't know David Gajic. I didn't know Andjelkovic. I only knew of him through the media. So practically speaking, Lukic was the only one that I sort of knew because I became acquainted with him one month prior to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you have Mr. Djordjevic's first name is -- I think it's translated here as Rodoljub; is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see the man that attended that first meeting here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you point him out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The gentleman in the last row sitting next to the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have his name down as Vlastimir. Where did you get the name Rodoljub? Pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was General Pavkovic who told me that. Actually, I'm certain of that because I wasn't sure. I would normally just note down the person's last name, and I think it was him - I don't know based on what and for what reason - told me this name. But this is definitely the man who is here in this courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how you came to put the names in this particular order that they're in with Mr. Minic as first and you as last? Was there any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not put them together in this way, except that I did the designation from the instructions of General Pavkovic because he knew who occupied which political function at the federal level, the political establishment, the police, and the army, and he dictated it all. He dictated Mr. Minic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, then himself, then Mr. Djordjevic, Lukic, Gajic, and I added myself at the end as one of those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us how you went about taking notes of the meeting. What was your usual procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of what General Pavkovic told me as to how to proceed, I decided to make note of things that I believed to myself as chief of department for operations and training needed in order to make certain evaluations, to draft certain orders related to army members. I'd like to emphasise that I made a certain analysis of this book because I made most of the entries. Most of the information was provided by the state security, Mr. Gajic and Mr. Radovic. Sixty to seventy per cent of the information originates from reports made by security organs to the other attendees regarding Siptar terrorist forces and the overall political situation, and it is the usual job of the state security to do this. And they would also provide information on possible impacts on members of the corps and members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand you were not trying to take a verbatim record of everything everyone said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Right, and that would have been impossible because some people speak fast, some speak slower. There are certain blanks because I couldn't understand certain words myself, and there are blanks that I filled in only later when during a break I had the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before today have you had a chance to examine this copy of your notes to see if there was anything that had been changed in the portions that you wrote back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the chance even before the trial of Milutinovic et al. last year and -- in fact, back in early 2008 I had the chance to examine my notes and see how many meetings were held, what subjects were the most discussed in terms of percentages. And I could not see, I could not find any corrections or modifications. I do not have any reason to believe that any alterations were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 136 in the B/C/S. I'll see if I can confirm the English page. I think we go to page 148 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you see that page in front of you in the B/C/S? I think the date is 14 October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you write the entry on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S then, I think it's 137, and then two pages or three pages further on in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when somebody else started taking the notes other than you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This page on the screen now, K022-8548, 21 October 1998, did you write that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 21st of October the note-taking was done by one of my assistants, Colonel Ratko Tesevic, and pursuant to an order by General Pavkovic I was engaged on another assignment at the time because the arrival of the OSCE mission was being prepared for in Kosovo, and I had to deal with that, whereas Tesevic took over the note-taking and attended briefings with General Pavkovic and he also attended exchanges of information between civilians and army members. And as far as I know, he worked at five meetings. And just before I arrived I once contacted Tesevic and asked him to confirm that he had indeed attended the previous meeting and he did. He even archived these documents, the first documents, and that's why you see the typing in the header, minutes of the Joint Command. This is not something I wrote. It was computer printed when the whole collection was made, and that was in October 1998, that was done with all the documents developed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you had the chance to examine those last few pages regarding the meetings from 21 October until I think the last meeting reflected is 30 October 1998, to verify that they were done in the handwriting of Tesevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I checked. It's his signature, and he attended these five meetings. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Handwriting not signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this time I would like to tender Exhibit P886. I think it's only been marked for identification up until this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you know the number with which it has been marked, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it was marked as Exhibit 886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will now become an exhibit of that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when you were here in I think May of 2008 to testify in the Milutinovic case, did you have occasion at the request of I think myself and Judge Bonomy to go through these notes and help us identify certain portions that the translators had not been able to read and had transcribed or translated as being illegible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that opportunity and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I show you now what is 65 ter number 04298. Do you recognise that, General?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to look at that -- a copy of that entire document before today and satisfy yourself that those were the changes you made in May of last year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have the chance to do that now, but I can see the things I entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you need to look at it any further to satisfy yourself that those were the changes you made?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am sure from the handwriting. I couldn't fail to recognise my own handwriting, regardless of the text. And if there's a problem I can help give you the answer. I'm sure this is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1217.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, there were a couple of items from the notes you took in 1998 that I wanted to ask you to elaborate on briefly if you could. At page 23 of the Exhibit 886, that's page 23 in both the English and the B/C/S. General, this is a meeting from the 30th of July, 1998. And if in the B/C/S you could go down near the bottom of the page you see General Djordjevic's name and the last entry under his name in my English translation is written as: "Munja will tomorrow proceed to Vucak near old Sarajevo ..." Do you know what "Munja" was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be 100 per cent sure, but I believe it is a unit from the area of Pec that was known in our jargon as Munja, or perhaps it was a person that the members of that unit nicknamed Munja, which means lightning, because of some physical abilities or skills. It was perhaps a unit of the MUP that was engaged in the area of the Vucak village facing Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honours, I think the correct English page is page 31. I have an earlier English translation with a different number. My apologies to the Registry officer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Next I would like to go to the meeting of the 20th of August, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, I need a moment to find my notes and the correct page number. The ERN in the B/C/S is K022-8466, and I believe that's page 65 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is from a meeting of the 20th of August, 1998. At the bottom of your page there's an entry for General Djordjevic, and I'm interested in the last two entries under his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the English I think we have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read those out for us and tell us if you know what they refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The last two points say: "720 have applied to the Ministry of the Interior." And the next point: "There are about 15.000 members." This refers to the fact that the MUP staff, in view of the current situation, opened a competition for the admission of new members from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and by the 20th of August a total of 720 applications had been received. And the second item just notes that there are about 15.000 personnel. I believe this is the figure for the total MUP personnel, but I don't know in which territory. I do not rule out the possibility that it means there are 15.000 conscripts not yet assigned. But I'm more inclined to believe it means there are 15.000 MUP personnel in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in total, including the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think when we looked at this document on Friday and Sunday there were a couple of entries we asked you about where General Djordjevic on one or two occasions made reference to the necessity to force some villagers to return to their homes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us why that was being done, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic -- please, excuse me, General. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I heard -- I'll tell you which kind of interpretation. I do not mind that this is a cross-examination, but Mr. Hannis says on Friday or Sunday Mr. Djordjevic told you that the villagers should be forced to go back home. I don't think that's appropriate. If there was a problem -- the question should still not put this as a statement. I think the witness should be the one to give us the answer as to what really happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Introducing a radical idea, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Hannis, you've heard that, and I'm sure you will take note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will adjust accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you specifically to another page in your notes. I think it's page 75 of the B/C/S. It's ERN K022-8486, it's a meeting of the 4th of September. Yes, do you see that entry for General Djordjevic and item number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's page 86 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My English translation says: "Return all inhabitants to the village by force tomorrow" or "all inhabitants are to be returned to the village tomorrow with the use of force." Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In order to explain this, to explain the context to this sentence, I have to say that when combat operations are to be carried out, the army and the MUP and the Ministry of the Interior are duty-bound to remove the civilian population from the area of combat and to inform them in advance. So the civilians, the villagers, were informed in advance by the army and the MUP and they fled to the woods themselves, men, women, children, all. And then it was a big problem for them to go back home because they were still in fear. And the psychological pressure on the Albanian population was huge. They were constantly told that the army and the police would mistreat them, harass them, kill them; they were never told the truth, namely that the authorities wanted them to go back to their homes and live a normal life. And out of this fear the villagers would stay in the woods for days and nights on end and would not dare to go back home. And in the meantime their houses were looted by other Albanians because the army and the police of Serbia were not able to even enter some of those villages. So General Djordjevic said that if they still did not want to go back home after being asked nicely and after all the explanations, they had to be made to go back because they couldn't stay in the forest with all the women and children and infirm people. I heard General Obrad Stevanovic speak of an example when two policemen had brought a baby, an infant, two or three months old, they brought this baby to the village to be fed before returning it to the mother. And only then did the mother realise it was her mistake to have kept the baby in the woods for such a long time. And that's the context of this order, they should be forced to go back to their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask a question related to that. Right above that entry General Lukic is noted as a speaker. And you see the second item under his name, and I have translated as: "Civilians were returned to the villages and able-bodied men have been kept." Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I see what General Lukic was talking about. It follows up on the previous sentence: "There were civilians who turned a deaf ear to the warnings." And then the next item says: "Civilians were returned to the villages and able-bodied [realtime transcript read in error "baseball-bodied"] men were kept." Which means that able-bodied men who still carried weapons and able-bodied men who had been terrorists but had discarded their weapons were all tested by the paraffin glove test by the police to establish which among them had been using fire-arms. That was not the only instance when this was done. It was also done in other places, the paraffin glove test, to establish which terrorists had been in action and which had not. The former were detained and the latter were released to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The way it reads, it says that all able-bodied men were kept whether they were carrying weapons or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You could say that. I know that all those who carried weapons usually discarded their weapons, changed into civilian clothes, and pretended they were civilians, even though they had used guns before. The same thing happened in Prizren, and that's why MUP applied the paraffin glove test and detained those who tested positive. They were later prosecuted and the rest of the men were allowed to go home. Now, what happened with them later I can only guess, I suppose they would join the KLA again, take up arms again, and that's how it worked throughout 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if I could interrupt a moment before we lose it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 21, line 15, refers to "baseball-bodied men" in the quotation. The quotation origin appears to be military-capable men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I may have been reading from my other English translation. I had able-bodied, but if the correct translation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the one we have is military-capable, but certainly not baseball-capable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, although I would think most military men should be able to play baseball, maybe not well, but ... I thank you. I stand corrected. I'll try and speak more clearly for the court reporter and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to set aside the Joint Command notes for now and ask you a related question about Joint Command. In 1998, even before this first meeting on the 22nd of July, within the Pristina Corps were you preparing some kind of reports that were called Joint Command operational reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what those were and what their purpose was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Before any meeting took place on the 22nd of July, in view of the situation that prevailed since March, we made our assessment in a way of the situation, and we decided that it was becoming more and more complex. Then sometime in late July, I think, through exchange of information exclusively between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps, we acquired information relating to members of the MUP - and that is the police - as well as the information from the State Security Service. General Pavkovic told me that that was pursuant to his agreement with General Lukovic [as interpreted] for them to provide us with certain information so that we can use it in making our assessment of the forces during the preparation of certain activities and in some other situations. So all this started long before this first official meeting of the 22nd of July. Also when MUP organs provided this information I ordered Colonel Tesevic to type this information, to feed it into a computer, and to add our information pertaining to the activities that we reported and informed the 3rd Army command, including our planned activities or the forthcoming activities that were included in the report to the 3rd Army, that is the primary and the principal task, the securing of the state border, the prevention of smuggling of arms, et cetera, all the regular army duties. Tesevic would compile all this information, and we would forward it to the Ministry of the Interior so that they would have a rough idea about what our major tasks would be in the next two or three days, just in general terms, training of soldiers without going into any specifics. So Tesevic did that, compiled such reports, and these documents were sent out without any signature because it did not have any operational value. It was only for filing purposes. It also served us as a basis for making an analysis for a certain period vis-a-vis both our activities and the terrorist activities, because the majority of the information was related to the state service, that is to say the intelligence and counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could show you a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have a look at 65 ter number 01197. And if the usher could assist me, I'll hand a hard copy to the witness which may make it go a little faster as we go through pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I think you may have seen this document before. The first page appears to be just a cover sheet with a name written on it. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's written on that first page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see. This is Colonel Tesevic's handwriting, the same handwriting that we see in the last notes in my notebook, and it says, "to Milomir Minic personally." This is the gentleman who was listed at the first meeting under number 1 among the attendees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page and the first of typewritten text in the B/C/S. This is a report dated the 20th of November 1998, the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 1142-134, operations report. Is this the standard format for these reports that you see in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the standard format, although it hasn't been prescribed by anyone or -- nor were any instructions were issued in that sense. There's no rule governing how these kind of documents are to be drafted because this kind of document was not an obligatory document for the command to produce nor does it contain any orders. It only describes what was happening in the past few days or in the last 24 hours and what was to be done next. Even when there were no meetings we exchanged information with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to whom were these reports circulated, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: One copy would be retained at the Pristina Corps command. I know that another copy would be sent by Tesevic to the MUP staff. And he also would send copies to certain individuals who were away from Kosovo for a long time. Those were mostly civilians because Mr. Minic was often away. And on a couple of occasions we sent some information to him, information of this type. And this particular one pertains to this period, and it was sent to him as [indiscernible] had explained to me to the office where Andjelkovic was as the representative of the civilian defence in Kosovo and Metohija as a member of the provisional Executive Council. So he sent this report, or rather, left it on his desk on the premises that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this number 1142, was that the number that referred to Joint Command matters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: 1142, yes, this is a number taken by -- on the basis of the same principle just like for any other document, in order for us to know how many such documents were produced. The main number is 1142, and 134 refers to the last in order that was recorded and was prepared at the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were these -- how often were these issued, every day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, every day. As I said, this did not depend on the meetings of the Joint Command. This was an exchange of information between the MUP staff and the army which took place on a daily basis. If you look at the army tasks and the engagement of army units, it's a copied version of the tasks that was sent to the 3rd Army. So we didn't provide any other information apart from the one that was supplied to the army. So the tasks are identical and one can check that in regular reports that were being sent to the 3rd Army command, and you can see for yourself that these tasks are identical to the ones received by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just quickly, on the first page item number I, Roman numeral I, is the intelligence and security situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the next page, Roman numeral II is the activities of the terrorist forces against the army, against the MUP, and against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Roman numeral III is the engagement of the army and the engagement of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Roman numeral IV is a proposal for further engagement of the army and of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the format that was used in each of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: More or less, yes. It was us who established this format at the corps command because we thought that this would cover all the issues that were of relevance for our exchange of information in order to avoid daily meetings. So we can see what the general tasks of the MUP were. Although this does not give us any detailed information, we can see, roughly speaking, what are the principal tasks of the MUP and vice versa. They could have familiarised themselves with our global tasks but without going into any particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the last page at the end, it's just a typewritten name, "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." No signature, no stamp. Is that how each of these reports ended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, each of these documents was sent in this form. I explained this in my previous testimony, that I considered the Joint Command to be composed exclusively by the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps. That was the only thing relevant to me because we were the only ones exchanging information on a daily basis. This was our duty under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it typical for a VJ document not to have a signature or a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, there are some such instances if -- it's not typical, but if a document is for information only it does not have to be signed, and it can only be for certain individuals and their eyes only as information to be used by them. However, if an order is contained in a document, it must be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to have just a quick look at four or five others just to tell me if these are part of the same series.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at 01198. Your Honours, I don't know whether it's more efficient for me move to tender that one now. I want to do five of them, they're all the same, but it may be easier to do them one at a time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One at a time, I think, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I will tender 01197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the usher could assist me, I will give General Djakovic a copy of this one, and I will get the other one back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, General, the first page appears to be just a cover sheet with Mr. Minic's name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could go to the next page for the typewritten transcript or the typewritten script.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is number 1142-136, two numbers up in the series and dated the 23rd of November. And do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. It seems to me to be the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you see it has a different date and a different number. The last one was November 20th, and it was a --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The format is the same, and also it says in handwriting to Minic personally, but I see now that the date is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And any reason to think that that's not an authentic copy of one of your Joint Command operative reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is not a report -- although it said in the heading "Joint Command," this document was actually prepared at the corps command based on the information received from the MUP and the army. I have no reason to suspect that this is [as interpreted] an authentic document because they practically have the same form, so there is no reason for me not to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender 01198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If the usher could assist, I'll make another trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, another one. Same question for you: Does this appear to be another one in the series?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same document, one of the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this 01203. And the date on that one, General?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: 15th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender 01203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It, too, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1220, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two more, General. This will be 01204.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also part of the series?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the date on that one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: 28th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 01204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one, General --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1221.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last one, General, looks like it's dated the 17th of October. This is 01206. Same as the others.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender 01206 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I would like to take a look at 65 ter number 01064. Did you know a gentleman by the name of Petar Ilic in Pristina in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he, and where did he work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the Ministry of Defence, one of its sections that was in charge of Kosovo and Metohija. I think that was the department within the Ministry of Defence for Kosovo and Metohija which practically covered the area that was slightly smaller than the one covered by the Pristina Corps. So the zone of the corps and the ministry did not coincide exactly. I -- we had slightly larger area including Kursumlija and other parts. I knew him personally, and we met a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he work in the same building as you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was two floors above from us, because all the organs from the MOD and the Pristina Corps and the communications units, part of the communication units of the VJ General Staff were all in the same building for security reasons. We were mainly assembled in one location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you help me out with something here. We have in 1998 and 1999 in Pristina the VJ, the regular army, if you will; we have the MUP, who has uniformed policemen, some regular police, and some who sometimes engage in anti-terrorist operations or even combat in 1999. What are the Ministry of Defence units? Do they have any kind of uniformed personnel; and if so, how do they relate to the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those employed in the Ministry of Defence were mostly civilians. I'm talking about those who were in our building, and they were discharged on duties relating to the civilian protection. And they carried out their duties pursuant to orders that they received from the minister of defence from Belgrade. That was their sole task. They had an obligation like we did, like all the other organs in the territory, to exchange information at request or to provide information if required. This is was fully in compliance with the rules. I know that there was an Albanian among them. There were Muslims as well, Serbs, Montenegrins, et cetera. In some earlier period many more Albanians were there, but under pressure they left the Ministry of Defence, and only one, as far as I know, remained. They carried out their regular duties preparing the civilian defence and protection units for performance of their tasks that were issued to them by the Ministry of Defence. Very seldom they had contacts with us. This happened most often if we knew each other, and then we would exchange information. However, the Ministry of Defence was not involved in any activities directly or in any meetings that were held under the name of Joint Command nor in any other meetings that we had for that matter. If we exclude Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic who was appointed to the provisional Executive Council in charge of civilian protection and defence, as for the others we didn't have any contacts with Mr. Ilic and others except the contacts that we maintained on a friendly basis. And most often he was the one who would approach me. According to what he told me -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, and ask you a couple of specific questions. Did members of the civilian protection have a uniform that they wore when carrying out their duties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: They had some uniforms and some weapons. I know for sure that they had weapons and equipment for 30 per cent of their units in Kosovo. As for the other weapons and arms was -- it was withdrawn from Kosovo and Metohija because the units did not reach the required strength because there were not sufficient number of Serbs, Montenegrins, and Muslims to form these units. There were only Albanians, but the Albanians refused to take part in the civilians defence and protection. And I know that for sure because he personally told him that his staff had problems in performing their tasks relating to the civilian protection and defence because terrorists would shoot at civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, please. This is taking longer than I had hoped. If you could try and just answer my question, and then I'll go to the next one. The uniform that civilian protection had, can you tell us what it looked like and how it differed from a VJ or a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, there was no difference between them and the army. They only wore patches stating that they were members of the civilian protection and defence. I personally saw some of these units on the ground because our units were in their proximity, and that is how I noticed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that there was some difference between civilian protection and civilian defence. Can you explain to us what the difference was between those two kinds of units, or are they two functions for the same unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the best definition that you said, one and the same part of the Ministry of Defence comprised both these functions. Only some of them were involved in civilian defence. They wore -- were allowed to bear arms, and they could have used these fire-arms in order to defend post offices and other enterprises that were on the list for which the protection should be provided, such as bridges, petrol stations, et cetera. As for the civilian defence, they were not issued any fire-arms, and it was intended for fire-fighting, providing first medical aid, et cetera. And their duties were carried out just like any other units of the civilian protection that are established everywhere in the world, so they operate on the same principles. And there is also third part of this segment, and that involved early warning units in -- concerning certain situations on the ground. And that ranged from the level of municipality up to the Ministry of Defence, even up to the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade. So this hierarchy, vertical hierarchy, went from the municipality all the way to Belgrade when it came to the civilian protection and defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have a break now. We resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when we broke we just brought up this document which is 01064 from the 28th of July, signed by Petar Ilic. And you'll see in the first paragraph it says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija has issued instructions for the defence of inhabited places from the activities of the Siptar terrorists ..." Were you aware of these instructions being issued in late July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see that instruction immediately, but I saw it a bit later, and I'm sure it wasn't drafted at the Pristina Corps, that much I know, because in some way the operations organ of the Pristina Corps would have been involved in the drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a question about that. And if we could go -- well, before we go, I would like to tender this document, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received -- yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to introducing this document through this witness. This is not a military document at all. The units involved were not within the jurisdiction of the army; they were in the jurisdiction of the federal Ministry of Defence. That's what the witness said, and he said that he saw the document only later. So I don't see how it can be admitted through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, you'll see this is a cover letter for instructions for the defence of residential areas, a document, instructions for the defence of residential areas is, I believe, already in evidence as Exhibit P1051. It was identified and tendered through Mr. Cvetic, who testified that he had received those instructions. This document itself appears regular in form, and it has a stamp, it has a signature of a person that this witness has identified as working in the department or Ministry of Defence in his same building. And we think that's sufficient for admission of the document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received. It is a document of which there is no apparent basis for questioning authenticity. The witness was aware of it, not immediately but at about the time of its issue. It does not need to be a document of his own making or of his own immediate department for it to be sufficiently identified to enable it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1223.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if we could go back for a minute and look at your Joint Command notes, that's Exhibit P886, and if we could look at page 3 of, I think, both the English and the B/C/S. General, I will tell you this is the second page from the meeting of July 22nd, the first meeting you told us about. And you'll see item number 2 at the bottom of the page. I think -- I don't have the right English page. You see item number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read out the first two lines that are on the screen there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "There is a danger of attack against cities. Not a single town or city may fall into the hands of the Siptars. General Pavkovic will produce an instruction giving priority to crisis towns Pec, Suva Reka, Kacanik" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. It appears that General Pavkovic was to give instructions regarding the danger of attacks on towns. Doesn't that refer to these instructions for the defence of populated areas? This is from a meeting of 22nd of July, and we see instructions being sent out by Mr. Ilic on the 28th. It seems as though they're connected.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You could say they are connected, but I say with full responsibility here that as chief of operations I do not know that any of the commanders under me drafted this instruction. I reviewed the instruction, and I suppose - as I told you - that the instruction was in the possession in some form of the Ministry of Defence, including Mr. Ilic in his department. And the instruction was only adjusted to include certain modifications of names, and it remained a general instruction of the kind that used to be made in the former Yugoslav People's Army for schools and certain other organisations to set certain general requirements for the defence of towns and other populated areas. For anyone who understands about defence and organisation of defence, this is just a check list basically for organising a defence, lest the person in charge of organising forget something. That's why I saw it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. The word that was translated just now, I think, when you read it out in Serbian is "uputstvo," that's spelled u-p-u-t-s-t-v-o, and that appears to be in capital letters and underlined in your notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I underlined it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I get some help from the booth, is that translated as "instructions"? Your Honour, maybe you have to make that request, because it's translated in this document as "directions;" but when he spoke it now, it was translated as "instructions." And in the earlier translation that I had, it's translated as "instructions." And in the document we just looked at, Mr. Ilic's cover letter, which was just admitted as P1223, the word is "uputstvo," u-p-u-t-s-t-v-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we've had the translation that's provided now. We will take your question as a request for a review of the translation that's been given, and that in due course will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, can you tell me why that word was put in all capital letters and underlined?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain what we just discussed. Instruction, "uputstvo," instructions is a similar term, even in Serbian, "instrukcije." And that's how it was understood, an instruction to the persons to prepare the defence of towns against the Siptar terrorists. I think we can agree on that. Why I put this here, I'm trying to think now. It must have been interesting for me at some point to create an instruction. I suppose that I thought that at some point General Pavkovic, himself, would order me to make an instruction. I suppose I was -- I had my hands full doing other things. But whether he received this instruction or he discussed it with someone else, I don't know. But I'm convinced that the instruction you showed me earlier is an instruction from the Ministry of Defence. And in earlier times it was developed by the JNA, by people who were very familiar with this subject. And then we used it as cadets and junior officers for examinations. That's the origin of this instruction. Because it's not a decision that involves the employment of forces. This is just a guide-line, a direction, what you should do to prevent towns falling into the hands of terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure you answered my question. Did you put it in all capital letters and underline it because you thought that it was a task that you might have to do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I expected to receive an order to that effect from General Pavkovic, but he never gave me that order and I never asked him later whether it was necessary or not, and he gave me no further orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to look at a related document. This is 65 ter number 01065. General, this is another document from Petar Ilic, dated 28 July, again referring to instructions for defence of inhabited areas. And you'll see he talks about the Joint Command having issued instructions, but I have a question about a couple of things in this document. He makes reference to the OiO. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the third function that I explained, civilian defence is one, civilian protection is another, and the third one within the department of defence at the level of the SFRY is the service for observation and warnings, monitoring and reporting, that is. It monitors and reports on the activities of terrorists on the territory, and this information is delivered to this department for monitoring and reporting and is passed on through the ministry chain of command to -- up to Belgrade and is then made available to all the relevant factors who are concerned in various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you ever seen this document before today, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I would not have been able to see this document. I can only suppose that he had to sell -- to send such documents to chiefs of departments and subordinated commanding officers pursuant to assignments he received from the Ministry of Defence. It was shown to me during proofing, but I had not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It appears to have the same stamp and signature that we saw on the other document from Mr. Ilic. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to make this trial longer and bother anyone, but what's the point? It's -- the point is not in this instruction as it was with Witness Cvetic who said, I received it, and I know about it. But this witness is not concerned. It has to do with the Army of Yugoslavia and the -- and a certain service. He only saw it during proofing, and now the Prosecution is tendering a document from another organ, and the witness says, I suppose it's from elsewhere and I suppose -- I haven't seen it before. I don't mind documents being introduced through this witness, but perhaps documents from his own organ. I would like one single criterion to be established for admitting evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no single criterion for the admission of evidence, apart from relevance and reliability. And we have to evaluate reliability according to the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive this document, essentially the reasons given for the earlier objection will be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the record I would indicate that the numbering of the documents and the content relates them as well, which I think would add to your -- add weight to your decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1224.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, just one more related to this, and then I'll move on to another topic. This is 65 ter number 01067. This also is a document from Mr. Ilic in the Ministry of Defence, dated the 22nd of July, 1998. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I've never seen this document before, and I could not see it before. I had no access to documents of this kind unless somebody showed it to me in proofing, but I really did not see this document at all. That's what I explained. See point 1: "Immediately start checking the working order of radio stations with personal information on the heads of households ..." Because that's one of the fundamentals of the system of the service for monitoring and reporting; it is through these radio stations that information is passed on, on all issues that are relevant, both those regarding civilian defence and civilian protection and combat actions and terrorists, accidents, emergency situations, everything goes through this service for monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Although I did not know that it was defined in the first point, the first item of this. And through this order he orders that the radios be checked and that personnel be at the ready in case orders are received to activate these radio transmitters for the purpose of this service for monitoring and reporting. That's the purpose of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned earlier about the service for monitoring and reporting. You see in the paragraph above the word "order" that it mentions communications centres in municipalities with the OUP, O-U-P, department of the interior. Were you aware of the existence of these OUP communications centres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew. I was aware. Here you have several communications centres --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and right above that you see it talks about integrating communications in the municipal observation and reporting centres installed in the homes of Serbs and Montenegrins. Were there no communications centres in homes of Siptars? Were they only in the homes of the Serbs and the Montenegrins, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only suppose since I had been in Kosovo even before, prior to 1992; I was absent for a while and then I went back again. The Siptars refused to be involved in anything that had to do with defence, including the civilian defence and civilian protection, they completely ignored the whole system, and that's why he emphasises Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this exhibit now as well. I think it relates to the ones that have previously been admitted as well as the instructions, and P1051, I think, discusses OiOs and these communication and monitoring systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same objection, but let me say that I don't think the document is irrelevant. My only objection is to introducing it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It, too, will be admitted for the same reasons essentially.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1225.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you about the plan that was called the plan to combat terrorism. You're familiar with that plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which plan you have in mind. You're talking about the general plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A plan that was referred to as the plan to combat terrorism --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how it was called, the plan to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and I'm familiar with that plan under this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Judges how -- when and how that first got started?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This plan started being drawn up sometime in June. There was some specific actions taken at the time. It started with a proposal for engagement of military forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in order to combat terrorism, and for that reason the first draft was called the proposal for the plan to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. So roughly speaking, it took place in June. That is when we carried out some more extensive assessments and valuations because the terrorist activities were of such intensity that they held control of 50 per cent of Kosovo. Three main roads were totally closed which cut off the supply lines, and for that purpose the army started making this plan. It was followed by certain activities and coordination with the MUP staff which took place in early June. And I suppose that parallel with us they carried out their own activities in compliance with their own specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said it started with the proposal, and then you began working on the plan. Was -- were you aware of a meeting that took place at the end of May where there was first discussion about such a plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that from General Pavkovic on the way to Belgrade, that I think on the 30th of May a meeting was held in Belgrade, and that these overall problems in Kosovo were discussed; and in a way that is when an initiative was launched to make certain preparations in order to monitor the situation so as to avoid any surprises either for the army or the MUP or other authorities in Kosovo relating to the forthcoming activities expected to be carried out by Siptar forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what Pavkovic told you about that May 30th meeting, where was it, who was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember him saying, because I insisted to hear who attended the meeting, and he told me that the meeting was in the president's office or with the president. I didn't insist any further on that, and that present there were certain MUP organs, representatives of the army, and government officials, certain government officials. I then insisted on him telling me exactly who there was, and then he gave me the names. As far as I can remember of all the persons mentioned here, I think that Mr. Sainovic was not present at this first meeting with President Milosevic, whereas the others were, and that included Stanisic as the chief of the State Security Service; Minister Stojiljkovic, the minister of the interior; General Lukic, as the commander of Kosovo staff; General Djordjevic; General Obrad Stevanovic; and from the army General Perisic, Chief of General Staff; General Dimitrijevic, chief of the security administration; and as for the civilians, I only remember that Mr. Sainovic was absent, and I think that all the others were there, although I must admit I wasn't much interested in that section as I was in the representatives of the army. And of course General Samardzic was there. I omitted him earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that meeting, did you in the Pristina Corps do any works -- any work on a proposal for this plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: General also told me that the Supreme Defence Council was going to issue a decision on the use of force. I think that took place on the 9th of June, but I learned about that some seven or eight days later. So roughly speaking on or around 15 or 20th of June, we, in the operations organ, started thinking about how to engage our forces in the event of an armed rebellion and some high-intensity clashes. That was in line with our rules of service, and it is particularly the duty of the operations organ to constantly monitor the situation, and in keeping with that, record the situation and make proposals to the command structures in order to rectify some emergency situation. This organ was particularly set up for these purposes, and it also involved other command organs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you and your team then draft up a proposal; and if so, what did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Once we received an order for this to be done, we recorded on a daily basis the activities of Siptar terrorists on -- in a map. And then after that we carried out an extensive analysis at the level of the corps command pursuant to General Pavkovic's order. But I asked him that if possible I receive information from all the structures operating in the territory of Kosovo for this analysis to be veritable and for avoiding any unconfirmed information. Therefore, we received information from the MUP, the State Security Service, the brigade commanders, the military district; in other words, from all the structures that I thought, along with the staff organs, can provide relevant information. And in this we involved the corps command to prepare this analysis. Our estimate was that there were between 22 and 25.000 Siptar terrorists of the manoeuvring structure, which means that they were capable of carrying out certain activities against the army and the MUP. And this information, as far as I know, was presented to President Milosevic and the political and state leadership in Belgrade on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 21st of July when this was presented to President Milosevic, do you know who was present? Was there some sort of meeting, or was it just mailed to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting attended by representatives of the MUP, the army, and other state officials, because all the state officials were up there. None of them were in Kosovo yet, only General Lukic and General Pavkovic. And on the 21st of July none of those that I mentioned before -- I was not personally acquainted with them. As I told you, I saw Mr. Djordjevic and the others on the 21st of July for the first time. I'm referring to the names who are on the first page of this list that the Joint Command kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
