utterances.text: Yes, those eight names including yourself and General Pavkovic, but that was on the 22nd of July; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm talking about the 21st of July now. That's one day before. And objectively it was impossible for me to be there. General Pavkovic had just arrived in Belgrade. General Lukic presented his plan relating to the deployment of military, what they were capable of doing realistically, and then a decision was made to make a plan for the use of force in order to break up the terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, on the 21st of July at that meeting in Belgrade with Milosevic about the plan, of those eight people named in the first page of your Joint Command notes, everyone was there except you? The other seven were there at the meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just go case by case. I think Minic was there. Sainovic appeared for the first time. I think that Andjelkovic was there. Matkovic, but he's not on the list. Djordjevic, yes. Lukic, yes. Pavkovic, yes. Yeah, roughly speaking, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: So the same composition, General Perisic and General Samardzic were there. General Dimitrijevic, the chief of administration was there as well. Nothing changed, except that now Sainovic joined them as a new person. Now I'm telling you all this because I received this as indirect information. Also present there was Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister of the interior, and other officers of the MUP. I think Obrad Stevanovic was there too at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you a few documents that relate or make reference to the meeting and see if you can tell us anything about them. The first is 65 ter 04302. This is dated the 22nd of July, 1998, to the 3rd Army command from General Pavkovic. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was drafted personally by General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in it he's telling his boss, his superior, General Samardzic, that at the meeting with President Milosevic an order was given to implement the plan for combatting terrorism. And in the last sentence he says: "In view of the above, please work out in more detail the engagement of the Pristina Corps units in the implementation of the plan." As a civilian and a layperson, it seems rather strange to me. It's almost as though the subordinate officer is telling his boss what to do. Can you enlighten us any about that? Do you know what was going on here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to General Pavkovic practically every time when he came from Belgrade because that is how I received orders for the preparation of documents. Later, not on the 21st but later, he told me that there were some problems when General Samardzic is present at the meeting with President Milosevic. He never has any objections then, but once he goes down there he imposes certain conditions on certain activities. And for that reason already on the 22nd General Pavkovic made it known to him that President Milosevic had ordered certain activities to be carried out by the MUP and the army in Jasic and Junik, this is close to the border, and to lift the blockade on the Pristina, Pec, and Komorane and other roads. He also requested him to give me precise tasks for implementation because the general had certain objections to this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 04302 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to move to another document related to that one, and this is 65 ter number 04303. This is the following day on the 23rd of July. Have you seen this one before, General? Let me hand you a hard copy so you can see both pages at one time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a follow-up of this written exchange between Generals Samardzic and Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the number on this item is 1187-1; correct? I'm sorry, did you say yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll see in the last paragraph above the signature General Pavkovic is saying: "On the basis of the above, please approve the use of units according to this proposal and plan in the spirit of the order of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." It seems as though General Pavkovic finds it necessary to invoke President Milosevic's name to get General Samardzic to do something. Am I understanding that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why was General Samardzic reluctant about this, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the planned proposal was handed over to General Smiljanic on the 15th of July at the headquarters and he knew exactly the assessment of the Pristina Corps and what kind of proposals for the use of forces they made. Now, it was up to them to approve this use and to carry out the breaking up of terrorist forces at a certain time. Now, what was the intention of General Pavkovic? Probably this was due - and this is my opinion - to pressure that was exerted on General Samardzic by General Perisic and perhaps General Dimitrijevic to carry out certain activities in which they were involved to be slowed down or even suspended or suppressed for some reason. I don't know what the reason was. However, there were different opinions and views. Now, if you have 50 per cent of your territory under the control of terrorist forces and it's your responsibility to unblock the roads as an army command and you do nothing, then we the officers couldn't understand what was going on within the relations between the highest army leadership and the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 04303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next one, General, related to this is 65 ter 04304. And this is dated the 23rd of July, 1998, and it appears to be a response to that one you're just looking at because you'll see it makes reference to that document number 1187-1. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by its content, it is completely clear to me. The main objection was that we did not include in the plan exactly what we were going to present, and the plan, anyway, was not attended for it to contain every point where activities were going to take place, but rather general outline of the activities. Based on this plan, other combat documents are then made which contain precise locations where the Siptar terrorist forces would be attacked and broken up. So the plan was not supposed to give us all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd move the admission of 04304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1228, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Djakovic, were you aware that at that time, in July 1998, that there was a rift or a disagreement between General Perisic and some of his associates on one hand and President Milosevic about whether and how the army could and should be used in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as the chief of the operations and training, my duty was to study combat documents and other orders regulating the use of the army. Therefore, it was my duty to tell General Pavkovic what I proposed to be done, on the basis of which he would make decisions. We were command organs, and as such we proposed to General Pavkovic to raise the issue of the lifting of the blockade of the roads because that was within the jurisdiction of army command and commander. It was his prerogative to provide supply to the Pristina Corps as well as to all other units and to secure that other activities of the army can be carried out unhindered. According to the Rules of Service, General Perisic had the right to use special army units in order to break up terrorist groups in Kosovo; that included the police and the special 72nd Brigade. And we invoked this in our presentation; however, none of this materialised. Then when the problem became so serious and that we had 50 per cent of the territory under their control, we were not capable with the existing forces to break up 25.000 terrorists who were well familiar with the territory, who were young, healthy, and well trained and with whom not even the army, regardless of how well equipped it was, could handle. And that included the MUP units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But General Perisic had a different view, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard he said once officially during the briefing in Pristina that his proposal was to introduce a state of emergency in Kosovo, to carry out mobilisation, and then proceed with the breaking up of the terrorist forces but only after a state of emergency or the state of war was introduced. So that would constitute a legal basis for that, although he could have used some other regulations in order to effect this, other than the state of emergency. But this is my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The plan to combat terrorism, I think, from other -- when you testified in Milutinovic, you had a discussion with Judge Bonomy about the phases of the plan. How many phases were there? Was it three, or was it five? And can you tell us how those came into being and what they were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I already testified to this, and I said in answer to Mr. Bonomy's question about the number of stages, I said the following: Initially the plan had three stages; and then subsequently, which was precipitated by the situation which developed in October and November, additional two phases were added. And now I can explain these stages to you. The first stage, as far as the army was concerned, was to break up Siptar terrorist forces in the border areas. Therefore, on the 21st of April, 1998, an IKM was established in Djakovica headed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name of the officer who was in charge of the IKM --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreter was asking you to repeat the name of the officer who was in charge, and could you also explain what IKM means. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was General Lazarevic, Vladimir Lazarevic, Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, who was in charge of the implementation of the first phase of the plan. And the IKM stands for forward command post, which was set up or is normally set up pursuant to an order of a commander of a certain unit for the purpose of carrying out tasks because of the distance between Pristina and the border which, roughly speaking, exceeds 100 kilometres. And due to inability to effect command, General Lazarevic was in the barracks in Djakovica, and he commanded these forces as stand-in officer for General Pavkovic. The second stage involved the breaking up of the Siptar terrorist forces in concert or, rather, by providing support to MUP forces in breaking up the Siptar terrorist forces within the area 10 to 15 kilometres from the border, from the state border. In other words, along the line Pec-Djakovica-Prizren. Since this road was blocked, the main task of the MUP was to deblock it, and the army was to provide support. The third stage involved providing support to MUP forces in lifting blockade of the main roads which lead from Kosovo to Metohija, and these were Kosovska Mitrovica-Rudnik-Pec road, Pristina-Klina-Djakovica road, and one section to Pec as well, and a third road was Stimlje-Suva Reka-Prizren. And that's where this initial proposal of the plan should end. But later, as the situation developed and as these Siptar forces kept moving constantly, avoiding direct conflict, direct clashes, and appeared in other new places, a plan was developed to include the fourth stage, breaking up their forces in main centres, Srbica and Cicavica mountain, in the area of Mount Jablanica and the broader area, including Glodjane village, where, according to our information, Ramush Haradinaj was the commander. And breaking up their forces in the area of Jezero mountains, Dulje, and the mountains behind Dulje where new forces were appearing. That's the fourth stage. And the fifth stage was developed at the moment when it was decided to send an OSCE mission to Kosovo, and in keeping with the agreement between the OSCE and our authorities certain forces were kept on the border, all the three border battalions in full combat-readiness. Also, seven combat groups who were tasked to provide security behind the border belt on the roads, mainly Djakovica-Prizren and Djakovica-Pec, plus three mixed companies in the area of Volujak mountains, that's the broader area of Klamovik [phoen] near Klina, one mixed company near Iglarevo, that's on the Pristina-Klina road. And a third mixed company in the area of Dulje to keep the road open. As far as I know, the MUP was tasked with setting up patrols and certain check-points, and I believe there were, all in all, 24 check-points. In any case, we put all of these check-points on a map that was kept as the working map for us, and I believe we did our job and the MUP staff did their job. So that was the fifth stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Related to that, I'd like you to look at 65 ter number 01435. And I know that some of the phases of the plan were discussed in those Joint Command meetings that you kept notes of, correct, from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say this: When he said this he did not mean this specific plan because not everyone was familiar with the exact sequence. They were only aware of certain stages, but they didn't know that a particular stage was the first or the third or the fifth. So they did not keep it in strict order like we did. For them it was just a number of stages, and the numbers did not necessarily coincide with the real numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Because they didn't have the plan before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me have you look at the document that's on the screen now dated the 22nd of September, 1998, from General Pavkovic in the Pristina Corps command. And it's entitled: "Implementation of stage five of the plan to combat terrorism." Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show me the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have a hard copy. If we can get you to the bottom of the page or the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I always try to see whether I wrote the document myself or some other organ did. When I wrote something myself, I know exactly what it is at first sight. And when somebody else drafted it, I still have some sort of recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This fits in basically with what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is Pavkovic writing about what was discussed at a meeting in Belgrade at the end of August, where the fifth phase was talked about; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 01435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit P1229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, when VJ units were carrying out certain anti-terrorist actions pursuant to the plan, were they required to report about those activities, particularly the ones that were done jointly with the MUP, report up to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commanders were required to send daily combat reports, and, from time to time, in seven- to ten-day intervals they provided summary reports about the activities of the army and the MUP, if they had any contact with the MUP, such as joint action, coordination, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter number 01420. Related to that last question, General, is a document that I think you've seen before. And it's dated --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this document myself, and I'm well familiar with the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is requesting information from the subordinate units about activities between 25 July and 6 August and activities carried out in conjunction with MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I move to tender 1420, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P1230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, if we could look next at 65 ter 01423. Did you get reports back from the subordinate units in response to this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we received it from all units; we received them regularly from all units. Not a single unit could fail to submit reports, and they had to follow a check list of issues to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 7th of August, 1998, from the 15th Motorised Brigade, and this is one of those -- this is an example of one of the responses you got; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: There's one mistake here, perhaps in the translation. It's not the 15th Mechanised or Motorised Brigade, as the interpreter said, it's the 15th Armoured Brigade, the 15th Armoured Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's my fault, not the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: So, yes, it's one of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My fault, not the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I move to tender that exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in the -- during the course of this plan in late summer 1998, I assume there were orders issued for activities to be carried out by VJ units in conjunction with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: An example, Your Honours, I think in evidence already is P890.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I'd like to show you another one, General, this is 65 ter number 01428 and ask you if you're familiar with this one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Dated the 14th of August, 1998, for breaking up Siptar terrorists in the Slup and Voksa villages sector. Do you need to see the rest of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No need. I personally took it to General Samardzic for approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see handwritten what's translated as "MUP forces." Do you know who made that change on the document, "SNAGA MUPA" I think is the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the handwriting, I would say it's General Pavkovic. When he checked the document, as a superior officer, he had the right to make certain corrections that do not change the substance before signing. And this one doesn't change the substance because General Samardzic did not want to approve a single decision that did not contain the phrasing "support the MUP forces." I was personally present when he ordered that MUP forces be drawn in green on maps and the phrase be included in the document. So that MUP performs the operation and the army acts in support. This was done probably because the typist omitted these two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see, General, that this order was signed by General Lazarevic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I just said, General Pavkovic told General Samardzic to go to the forward command post where General Lazarevic was. And when he was there I asked him, Did you make the plan, Pavkovic? He said, Yes. Who can bring it for approval? He said, Djakovic. And then he said, Okay, let Djakovic bring it and you go to Lazarevic and deal with these problems. I don't know what the problems were. And when the plan was approved, I passed on the decision to the forward command post, to General Lazarevic, and he, since he was the one leading the operations, signed it, signed the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I remember in your Joint Command notes that there was a discussion where Pavkovic mentioned that General Lazarevic was going to be delegated or designated to lead this particular operation, is that right, in Slup and Voksa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Since it was called order and Lazarevic was down there, he was in command not over large, strong forces, but he had constant insight into the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English if we could go back one page, to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 6, General, in your B/C/S page on the screen, it talks about command. And it says that the operation is to be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Can you explain why that was in there? Who was commanding? Was it General Lazarevic in the VJ, or was it the Joint Command which was something else? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps during my last testimony, I explained in much greater detail how this part came to be, how the term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" came to be. And it was related to the arrival of persons who were present on the 22nd. In the computer there must have been a template for all types of command orders, and the operator probably kept this term "Joint Command." As far as I know, General Lukic was in Pristina and he had an office there where he received reports from his underlings. General Lazarevic was at the forward command post in Djakovica, and he would go into the field from time to time as required. General Pavkovic was in Pristina, in his command post, in the building of the command. I don't know that anyone else anywhere else formed a command that governed combat operations. From what I saw, General Lukic was in charge of the MUP, and General Pavkovic and Lazarevic were in charge of the activities of the corps after their decisions were approved by Samardzic. Why they put "Joint Command" on documents over a long time, I don't know. They probably wanted all the participants to know that the activities had been harmonised and coordinated between the army and the MUP. That's how I understood these documents when I received them. So for the most part it was General Lukic or perhaps somebody he authorised like a detachment commander or another commanding officer that he authorised. One of his assistants or his deputies could have led this operation together with General Lazarevic, but I don't know of any specific instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't you testify earlier that you personally delivered this one to General Samardzic ? Did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The decision, the decision that needed to be approved. It was a decision on a map. I believe the Office of the Prosecutor has that map. I have seen it, in any case, I think at the Milutinovic trial. And in the right top corner, if you remember, there is writing that says "decision, approved, General Samardzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you in the summer of 1998 ever see any of those documents that had that term, "Joint Command," in it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in nearly all documents, but it didn't bother any of us because we thought it meant that the coordination between the army and the MUP had been completed. Certain organs asked me about that at the time, and I explained that it only meant that coordination had been completed between the army and the MUP as a required element in combat operations. It doesn't mean that they could do anything just on the basis of this Joint Command document without receiving orders from their directly superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you 65 ter 01440. While we're waiting for that to come up, was there an obligation of the J -- commanders to report up the chain whenever they learned about any crimes that may have occurred during the course of carrying out anti-terrorist actions or combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was prescribed by general rules. Even without a specific order, he was required to inform his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before I ask you a question about this one, could I tender the last one we were looking at, 01428?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General, this one we're looking at, 1440, have you seen it before? It's dated the 5th of October, 1998. I can give you a hard copy so you can see all three pages at once in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the contents and the problems described here -- I mean, I am aware of the problems dealt with in this document, but I have not seen it before. It was done at the level of General Pavkovic and other organs perhaps, because I dealt mainly with things that concern operations. But these reports on human losses and expenditure of ammunition, et cetera, that was not the job of the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In this one I'm not so interested about the ammunition issue, but in paragraph 2, that's on page 4 in the English version, and I think it's the second page in B/C/S, you'll see there's mention about an alleged massacre against the civilian population in the village of Gornje Obrinje on the 26th and 27th of September, 1998. Do you remember that there was some -- there was some public, domestic and international, media attention to this alleged massacre in Gornje Obrinje? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember some of these things, but I can't pin-point a time-frame, whether it was the 26th or the 27th. But I remember one thing. Once we had reports that allegedly in the tunnel where the train from Pristina passes on the side of Dobrinja there were many persons who were injured and dead, that personal items were strewn around, and General Pavkovic sent a unit, I believe, led by Lieutenant-Colonel Milicko from Pec, and he didn't find anything there that would indicate a massacre or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this incident with the tunnel, but I'm not sure it's the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. The same item under paragraph number 2, General Pavkovic reports about certain unchecked information, that the army security services had sent to the General Staff, indicating that unidentified members of some MUP units had executed persons that had been taken into custody. Do you recall, was that reported to the MUP by the VJ about this report that MUP members had executed people taken into custody? Do you know, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Exhibit P753 is in evidence. I think that was Mr. Abrahams who introduced that. That's a Human Rights Watch report about Gornje Obrinje, and I just bring that to your attention at this point in time because it relates to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Could I tender that before we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now and resume at ten minutes past 6.00

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, I just wanted to advise you that I had advised Mr. Djurdjic during the break that I don't believe I am going to be able to finish today. I hope the Court will permit me perhaps to have as much as 45 minutes or an hour tomorrow to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Silence reflects our disappointment, but realistic assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do my best to get as much done as possible and not have much for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we've been talking about the plan and the five phases. We've talked about some meetings in Belgrade related to that plan. Were you aware of a meeting in late October 1998 that General Pavkovic attended regarding the plan to combat terrorism?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In October?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think on the 29th of October to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a vague idea about the date, but I know about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to hand the witness a hard copy of the exhibit that I'm going to talk about now. This is P087 already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this reflects the minutes of a meeting that's described as the operations Inter-Departmental Staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. Is that the meeting that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know this because these documents were available to me, but I will have to look at it because there's such a bulk of information for me to tell you specifically what it is all about. Therefore, I would like to hear a specific question from you. But, as I said, I know about this meeting in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you start at page 2 or at the -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have to be cautious here. This is a document, and it involves a meeting that the witness did not attend. I think it would be appropriate for examination-in-chief to ask witness first what he knows about this, who he heard it from, and then possibly about some information contained in the document. Let us first separate what he knows personally and what he learned from the document, and he will give opinion then. If you just read the contents of the document to him, that's informing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but I have the dilemma that I have shown the witness the document before during proofing and preparing, so he has seen it. So I don't want to mislead anybody about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you mentioned that you were aware of this meeting. How did you hear about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it from General Pavkovic because, generally speaking, I received information from him. Before every departure of his for Belgrade I have to prepare certain things, whether he has to present some maps or some written reports. Normally this would be very short addresses, two pages at the most, and it all related to army issues. And upon his return, he would just inform me that something was either approved or not approved and what has to be amended. Therefore, he had to supply certain information for me to be able to carry on with my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of information you provided to him to take with him when he went to the meeting, because I think you said that was part of what you did.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall if you prepared anything for General Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that. It is difficult for me to tell you this at the moment. I can only tell you what I know, and the reason is because in the course of these preparations for all kinds of meetings, not only those held in Belgrade, I never thought at that time and I never made a mental note of remembering because I never imagined that this would be needed in the future. I just told you that we had to prepare some short address, as I said, two pages, two and a half pages, dealing and addressing the issues relating to the army because the General spoke on behalf of the army for the most part. If he had to show a map we would prepare this map for him, and he would present it. Therefore, I would need a specific question from you, and I will respond and confirm or not confirm whether I or any other organ prepared something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what he told you when he returned from the meeting, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that I recall anything in detail that would remind me of what he told me upon his return. Sometimes one can remember things easily, but I'm not sure. This was already the end of the year. That's the period when the OSCE had arrived, when the terrorists had stepped up their activities sometime in December. I know what the situation was, but I don't know anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to something else then. I'd like to show you what's in evidence as Exhibit P889. This one will come up on your screen in a minute. I don't have a hard copy of it with me, but I'll tell you it's a document dated the 16th of February, 1999, from General Lazarevic. And you'll see the reference number is 455-1. It's an order to break-up and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what it is, what it was for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document during the previous trial of Mr. Milutinovic. I am aware of these activities that were carried out in the area of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo. This had been planned by the army relating to the use of the army units in these particular regions. This is a wide area. Malo Kosovo is the area of Podujevo, Drenica is Srbica, and Malisevo is a mountainous area. It's the whole belt that goes via Bajgora, Cicavica, to Malisevo, so it's a wide area encompassed by these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in this document under item number 1 where it talks about the enemy, paragraph number 2 says: "The STS," or Siptar terrorist forces, "biggest strongholds are in the areas of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, Malisevo" et cetera. This looks like this is an order to do what you described as phase four of the plan to combat terrorism, which, as I recall your answer, was phase four, was breaking up the terrorists or the KLA in their main centres. Am I interpreting that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not entirely. We are talking here about 1999. The fifth stage was completed in 1998. The General Staff issued a directive called Grom 3, and pursuant to it there was a basis for carrying out the activities of crushing the terrorist forces, including these activities. So this was done with the knowledge of the General Staff. The corps commander pursuant to this directive relating to Grom 3 which in one item says that for the breaking up of Siptar terrorist forces, they should be ready within three or four days, and they used this as the basis for planning because the Siptar terrorist forces had re-organised, re-structured, and were preparing armed rebellion in the spring of that year in the entire territory of Kosovo. So this has nothing to do with the five phases that we were talking about. This is an entirely new situation, and it has to do with Grom 3. I already mentioned this, and this had to do with the preparations for anti-landing activities in order for the Grom 3 to be fully implemented. Because without the implementation of these tasks there could be no implementation of the order relating to Grom 3. Because this is the first phase of preventing the bringing in of NATO ground forces and to break-up the forces that were deployed on the landing line. According to our rules, the basic task in that situation is to crush these terrorist forces, to occupy the positions, to fortify them, and prepare -- make preparations for the defence from the landing of NATO multi-national brigade. So in operational terms this is what is consistent with our rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Grom 3 was a different plan than this one, wasn't it? Because it specifically said it was directed at preventing the arrival or introduction of NATO forces into Kosovo. It's something separate and distinct from this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is closely related to it. The basic rule is that in the area where landing of the enemy forces is expected, you have to break up all terrorist forces and other special units in order for you to take up positions. Now, it was the battle of who is going to take up positions on the edge of this territory. Since the Siptars were holding the places --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I asked that question because I was under the impression that there was a separate document called Grom 3, but unless and until I find it, let's move on. Let me show you then a document that is 65 ter number 04141. Now, this is a document, General, that's dated just two or three days later in February 1999. And you'll see that the heading on this one is MUP command. It's dated the 19th of February, 1999. It has a blank for a confidential number. There's no signature on the last page. Have you seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's entitled: An order to break-up and destroy forces of the Albanian terrorists in the sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, Malisevo. So in the name of the order, in the description of the enemy and their zones of operation, it appears to be nearly identical to General Lazarevic's that we just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The format is identical, only General Lazarevic is giving specifics -- or rather, his operations and training organ has this template order on their computers, and by filling in on the blanks prior to certain activities they carried out. And the template of this order remained in the computer. This is what I did in the Pristina Corps because all the officers were there. Those people were working there and I know all of these men, and I was a kind of superior to them in professional terms, and I, myself, was also involved in some activities which I can explain later if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page of both the B/C/S and English versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see there's just a typed word "commander," and on the left there are some initials. Whose initials are those on the left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: MDj is my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's the author of this document? The first two initials are those of the author; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in this instance, because this is the template that was made back in 1998. It was only amended from time to time. That is why I have my initials as the author of this template. And as the situation developed, it was amended by adding specific information. So this is not an order in itself. It's just a format of how you should write an order, and it is a kind of tool that helps you do certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And another difference between this document and General Lazarevic's which we looked at just before this one is that this one contains task for MUP units instead of tasks for VJ units; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for that was because we sent this document to the MUP units to enable them to use it if they thought that that could be helpful for them in a specific situation. So this was not an order. It was just a format in which we provided assistance according to combat rules is something like this to be done, and we just offered them an opportunity to make use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you testified in Milutinovic that that was because you in the VJ knew how to write combat orders because that's your job, and in the police they're not used to doing that. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's a basic thing in an army. You cannot carry out combat operations without an order. Therefore, the same should apply to the police. However, how they issue their tasks, it's their affair. I never said that we were authorised to control the police. They were nonetheless obliged to carry out certain tasks and to coordinate their activities, especially combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So did you physically prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I prepared this document, and you see that the command post of the MUP staff is in the peacetime building in Pristina, because on the 29th it was bombed. So on this particular date it was still in its old location. I ordered the computer operator to print this form for me and to send it to the duty service in order to be delivered to the MUP, without any obligation on their part vis-a-vis the army or vice versa. This was simply assistance provided to them because under the law our duty was to provide them with professional assistance particularly in the domain of training. And that was the duty of the army, both regarding the police and the civilian protection units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move to tender 4141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few more questions about Joint Command in 1999. I'd like to look at exhibit or 65 ter number 02003. General, this is an order dated the 2nd of April, 1999. I don't know if you will recall that General Lazarevic's order of February 16th, 1999, that you described as being Grom 3-related bore the number 455-1. So this document appears to be related to the same theme or the same general topic. And this is an order to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Jablanica sector. That seems that this is an order, then, to carry out part of what was described in General Lazarevic's February 16th order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask this document that -- the previous document that Mr. Hannis is referring to be shown, and that would help us to resolve this matter quickly. Well, I can say right now we're talking here about the Jablanica sector, and in the previous document there was Malo Kosovo and other sectors. And, Mr. Hannis, the numbers are not identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I leave that to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry if my learned friend understood me to be saying the numbers were identical, but the 455 is identical, and then I was just trying to suggest that 115 was a part of the series that the 16 February document in P889 is the first of, as 455-1. But I'll move on to a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is -- you'll see in the upper left-hand corner this is described as Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Did you see any of these Joint Command orders in 1999 shortly before and/or during the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said last year that I did not take part in the preparation of these documents in 1999, but I am aware of the activities that were carried out in Jablanica, Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo, which is mentioned in the 16th of February document. This was part of the activities that were basically related to Grom 3, because Grom 3 specified the task, and now it was up to the corps commander to decide what the possible objectives of the terrorist forces would be and to carry out the tasks in compliance with the order issued. This is perhaps the third time that there was an attack on Jablanica, because Jablanica and Baranski Lug were a stronghold that the army and the police had failed to break-up practically until the end of June 1999. That is why this order relating to Jablanica, Bajgora, Malo Kosovo, Cicavica, et cetera, appears several times because the forces were constantly flowing in and coming back to the same area. You managed to destroy 10 to 15 soldiers and then 3 or 400 new soldiers emerge. That is why we have documents being repeated. This does not mean that these activities were not carried out because this order had to be carried out to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it wasn't carried out. My question, though, is: The number 455, the first one that we saw, 455-1, 16 February 1999, signed by General Lazarevic was, I think, listed as a Pristina Corps document; and this one says "Joint Command." Do you know why "Joint Command" is being used for what appears to be a Pristina Corps reference number?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I understand the question. At the previous trial also I said that there was an order template in the computer, and people mechanically wrote "Joint Command" because the activities were harmonised between the army and the MUP and without this harmonisation and coordination, we were not able to go into fighting. The MUP, too, could have not supported the army where the army was the primary player in the activities. We needed to finish that part of the work before we proceeded to anything else, Radojko Stefanovic was in charge of coordination with all the entities on the territory, and he was also in charge of coordination with MUP units. Even when we are not acting together and we are not supporting them, we have to coordinate with them to avoid friendly fire. And the number appears because -- you see, it says 115 here, and it used to be 1. There were many other orders that has nothing to do with using combat, and they are repeated under 455, like it was with the corps command, and here, the Joint Command. Basically this is an order from General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me, then, ask if we can go to the last page of both the English and B/C/S versions. And you'll see, General, that we don't have a signature. It just says -- there's a typewritten "Joint Command for KiM," Kosovo and Metohija. And on item number 11 on your copy, it talks about the operation being commanded by the Joint Command, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to go back one page in the English for Your Honours to see item 11 -- well, I guess it's at the very bottom -- I'm sorry, if we could return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the very bottom it says: "The Joint Command for KiM from the Pristina sector shall command and control all forces during the combat operations." Do you see that, General, the last sentence above the signature block?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why this Pristina Corps document isn't signed and makes reference to the action being commanded by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only reason could be that one of the brigade commanders was the main person in charge of certain combat actions. I always told you that in my mind Joint Command was the MUP staff and the command of the Pristina Corps. There could have been coordination between them, and that coordination had to be confirmed to the MUP units, because MUP units did not want to carry out any activities unless they have received confirmation that coordination had been done between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps under the name Joint Command. And they consistently refused any such thing in the area of the 125th Brigade. The chief of SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica would always say, I did not receive any orders from the MUP staff, although he had in his hands the document headed -- titled "Joint Command." But whenever he would receive orders from the MUP staff, then this person Cvetic -- sorry, when the commander Cvetic received orders from the Pristina Corps, then he would make no problem in providing support to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an objection. It's a comment on the transcript. Could the witness please repeat this part concerning who Cvetic received orders from before he was willing to act.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Cvetic and all our commanders, operation commanders of brigades, reported that if SUP secretaries or special units of the police detachments and companies had not received assignments from the MUP staff in the form of document headed "Joint Command" or a dispatch -- I don't know how it worked with them. I know only about our documents, our units received orders Joint Command for the KiM, and they would communicate it to all the SUPs. But if they did not receive orders in that form, then they were not willing to carry out the combat activities that had been planned. Once they had received them, then there was no other problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay -- I see Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again we have a problem. It's not the SUP, it's the MUP. Page 77, line 1, it's not S-U-P, it's M-U-P, at least it should be, the staff of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MUP staff is at the level where General Lukic was, but secretaries, as far as I know, were based in towns, Kosovska Mitrovica, Prizren, Pec, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. You see the transcript and if you're not happy with it, I suggest you use cross-examination to clarify any unsatisfactory point. We can't go on with this sort of intervention. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, just to be sure I understand, it sounds like you're saying that for these coordinated activities the MUP units would not have accepted an order directly from General Lazarevic and the Pristina Corps, somebody in the army, unless it was titled "Joint Command." And if it said "Joint Command," then they would follow along. Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they have to receive the order through their own chain, from the MUP staff down the line, as it worked there. So regardless of the fact that Zivanovic showed them the document, it was not relevant for them. Yes, they believed him, but they did not receive specific orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like next to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, could I tender that document, 02003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next if we could show the witness 01487.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a document from General Ojdanic in the Supreme Command Staff, dated April 1999. I think it's the 5th -- no, it's the 17th, the 17th of April, and it's to the 3rd Army command, to the commander personally, which would have been General Pavkovic at the time. It's -- it says "Link," and then it's a link to Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order number 455-148 of 15 April and it's entitled "Suggestions." Did you have a chance to see this document before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have a couple of just general questions for you. In your military career of 30 years, did you ever see a superior officer sending to a subordinate officer some document called "Suggestions"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you were a subordinate officer and received a document from a superior entitled "Suggestions," would you feel that you were under any obligation to follow what was in that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I received such an order called "Suggestions," it would not be binding. I could act upon it and then I could not. General Ojdanic made certain suggestions or I made certain suggestions, and the superior officer can accept them and may not. It's not binding. To be binding, an order has to be phrased with "I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what this is about? Do you know what the linked Joint Command order related to? And what operation or action that pertained to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was about certain activities in the Rugova gorge and the engagement of -- some requests had been made to engage the army, and I know for sure that the army was not engaged there, apart from a unit of -- from that military district which performed a blockade in the north-west part of Djakovica town. Their only mission was to prevent the entry of terrorist forces into the territory of Djakovica town, where they could hide. And as far as I know, this activity was carried out by units of the Ministry of the Interior. It's on the map, and there is a text also created for the Rugova gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: As a civilian and a layperson, it seems, though, that General Ojdanic - who was the highest uniformed officer in the VJ - is making suggestions about an order that came from the Joint Command. That looks like General Ojdanic is recognising the Joint Command as some sort of superior authority to him. Would you agree with that, or do you have some other explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This command could not be superior to General Ojdanic. There is no scenario in which it could be superior. As I see the situation, Ojdanic did not want to interfere directly with the execution of combat operations because it -- that is at the level of one combat group. And a Chief of Staff would have to lower himself five levels to do that. That is the job of lieutenant-colonel, a colonel at most. It would have been better if he had ordered simply, saying, I hereby order, otherwise he should have left it to the command to finish that job. Why he gave General Pavkovic the right to decide for himself what to do, I don't know. General Pavkovic must have used his own discretion. And the action itself had already been planned and may have even been under way at the time this arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I'll stop there because there's one administrative issue I want to raise with regard to an exhibit we used earlier. Could I tender this one, though, before we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P1236.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all I have for the witness. I can discuss this issue while he's here if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, if you're not troubled by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not a problem. It's Exhibit P886 which are the witness's notes of the meetings of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You noticed I was having problems getting the page numbers to match up. The English translation that is in e-court is an earlier non-CLSS translation, and what I had in hand is ERN 0308-5476 through 5619, which is the official CLSS translation. And what we would propose to do is substitute this updated CLSS official translation into e-court for the previous unofficial version, if Defence has no objection. That way we won't have to make a request for clarification about that translation issue that I raised concerning the Serbian word for "instruction" or "direction."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand a thing, but I trust the CLSS, and I see no problem in replacing the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The new authorised translation will be substituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And then if I may end for the day and have 45 minutes or an hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean you want to finish early, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'm at an appropriate breaking point, going to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a good breaking point. Very well, we will adjourn two minutes early. I'm afraid we must finish for the day now. We resume tomorrow at 2.15. We would ask you to be back then to continue with your evidence. The court officer will give you further specific assistance if you need them. Thank you. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
